articles.title: What is the NLE (NRE)?
lines: The National Licensing Examination (NLE) is the exam that doctors who qualified from a foreign medical college must pass before they can get a full licence to practise as a general practitioner in Pakistan. Under the PM&DC Act 2022, Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PM&DC) now calls it the National Registration Examination (NRE). Most candidates and coaching centres still say NLE; it is the same exam.
## Two components
- Theory (often called Step 1): 200 computer-based single-best-answer MCQs.
- Clinical Skills Examination (CSE, often called Step 2): an OSCE of 20 stations.
You must pass both components separately. Only candidates who pass the theory component can sit the CSE.
## What this app covers
This app prepares you for the theory component: 10 full-length mock papers weighted like the real paper, subject practice with explanations, and these rules and tips.
PM&DC can change the format, dates and fees. Your admit card and the official notices on the PM&DC website always come first.
## Official sources
This app is not a government app and does not represent PM&DC or any government entity. The exam information in this guide is summarised from PM&DC's official pages:
- PM&DC website: https://pmdc.pk
- NRE standard and syllabus: https://pmdc.pk/Publication/Syllabus
- NRE registration portal: https://nre.pmdc.pk

articles.title: Theory paper at a glance
lines: ## Format
- 200 MCQs, single best answer from the options given.
- Questions target higher cognition: applying knowledge to clinical problems, not just recall.
- 70% clinical sciences (140 MCQs) and 30% applied basic sciences (60 MCQs).
- No negative marking: a wrong answer costs nothing, so never leave a question blank.
- Pass mark: 60%. PM&DC also uses the Angoff method to standardise the exam.
## Clinical sciences: 140 MCQs
- Medicine and Allied: 52
- Surgery and Allied: 48
- Obstetrics and Gynaecology: 14
- Paediatrics: 14
- Ophthalmology: 6
- ENT: 6
## Applied basic sciences: 60 MCQs

PM&DC's 2024 standard lists Applied Pathology 11, Applied Anatomy 11, Applied Physiology 10, Clinical Pharmacology 8, Applied Biochemistry 6, Community Medicine 6 and Forensic Medicine and Toxicology 4. Those numbers add up to 56, not the stated 60, so this app's mock papers use 13 Pathology and 13 Anatomy to make a full 200-question paper.
## Timing

PM&DC's standard does not state the length of the theory paper. Candidates and prep providers report about 3 hours 30 minutes, so the mock papers here use 210 minutes. Check your admit card for the real timing.

articles.title: Eligibility and registration
lines: ## Who can sit
Graduates of PM&DC-approved foreign medical colleges with an MBBS, MD or equivalent degree (as listed in PM&DC's approved foreign degree nomenclature), who hold a provisional licence from PM&DC.
## Typical steps
- Get your provisional licence from PM&DC first.
- Create or log in to your account on the PM&DC online portal and apply for the announced NRE session before registration closes.
- Upload the documents asked for, usually your degree, transcripts, identity document (CNIC or passport) and photographs.
- Pay the exam fee online as instructed.
- Download your admit card (roll number slip) once your application is approved, and check your name, photo, centre and timing.
## Frequency
PM&DC holds the NRE at least twice a year, at several centres across Pakistan. Dates are announced, and sometimes moved, through PM&DC notices, so check the website regularly.

articles.title: Exam-day rules
lines: These are the usual rules for a computer-based licensing exam in Pakistan. Your admit card and the centre staff's instructions are what count on the day.
## Bring
- Your printed admit card.
- Your original identity document (CNIC, or passport for foreign nationals), matching the name on your admit card.
- Anything else your admit card lists. Leave everything else at home or in your car.
## Do not bring into the hall
- Mobile phones, smart watches, earbuds, cameras or any electronic device.
- Books, notes, papers, calculators or bags.
Being found with a prohibited item can cancel your result, even if you did not use it.
## Conduct
- Arrive well before the reporting time; late arrivals may not be admitted.
- Expect identity checks, biometric or photo verification and a security search.
- Do not talk to other candidates, copy, or help anyone. Raise your hand for the invigilator if your computer has a problem.
- Do not try to copy, photograph or memorise and share questions. Exam content is confidential, and sharing it is misconduct.
- Follow the invigilators' instructions about breaks and leaving the hall.

articles.title: Passing, validity and attempts
lines: ## Passing
- Theory: at least 60%.
- CSE: at least 60% overall, and you must pass all three mandatory stations. Failing even one mandatory station fails the CSE, whatever the total.
- You must pass both components to pass the NRE.
## Validity
A theory pass stays valid for five years. You must pass the CSE within those five years.
## Attempts
- There is no limit on the number of times you can attempt the complete NRE.
- If you pass theory but fail the CSE, you re-register for the CSE only.
- After three consecutive failed CSE attempts, you must sit both theory and CSE again.
## The CSE in brief

An OSCE of 20 stations, about 3 hours 30 minutes including the briefing. Each station has 8 minutes, with 2 minutes to change over. It tests interpretation of clinical and diagnostic data, diagnosis, management plans, examination skills and key procedures.

articles.title: A 12-week study plan
lines: Spend your time where the marks are. Medicine and Surgery together are half the paper.
## Weeks 1 to 4: Medicine and basic sciences
- Medicine by system: cardiology, respiratory, GI and liver, renal, endocrine, neurology, haematology, infectious disease.
- Revise the matching basic sciences alongside each system: anatomy, physiology, pathology and drugs.
- Do 40 to 60 practice questions a day and read every explanation, including for questions you got right.
## Weeks 5 to 8: Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Paediatrics
- Surgery: principles, trauma (ATLS), acute abdomen, GI, urology, orthopaedics, breast and thyroid.
- Obstetrics: bleeding in pregnancy, hypertension, diabetes, labour and PPH. Gynaecology: menstrual problems, infertility, contraception, cancers.
- Paediatrics: neonates, growth and the EPI schedule, diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition.
- Sit your first mock at the end of week 6, to set a baseline.
## Weeks 9 to 12: the rest, then mocks
- Eye, ENT, Community Medicine and Forensic Medicine: small but quick marks.
- One full mock each week under timed conditions, then a day reviewing it.
- In the last week, revise your weakest topics from the Progress tab. Do not start new subjects.

articles.title: How to answer single-best-answer MCQs
lines: - Read the last line first, so you know what is being asked: diagnosis, next step, investigation or treatment.
- Then read the stem for the key clues: age, sex, setting, timing, and the one abnormal result.
- Try to answer before looking at the options, then find the option that matches.
- More than one option can be true. Choose the BEST one for this patient at this moment. 'Next step' usually means the safest, most immediate action.
- Stabilise first: in an unwell patient, airway, breathing and circulation come before investigations.
- Choose the least invasive investigation that will answer the question, unless the patient is unstable.
- Watch the setting. A BHU without a CT scanner changes what you can do next; a referral may be the right answer.
- Don't overthink. Your first well-reasoned answer is usually right; change it only if you find a clue you missed.

articles.title: Time management
lines: - About 200 questions in about 210 minutes gives you roughly one minute per question, with a little time to spare.
- Do a first pass at a steady pace. If a question takes more than 90 seconds, pick your best answer, flag it and move on.
- Use the time left for flagged questions.
- There is no negative marking, so make sure every question has an answer before time runs out.
- Practise under the same conditions: the mocks in this app run on a timer, and the question map shows what is answered and flagged.

articles.title: High-yield themes for Pakistan
lines: The NRE tests whether you are ready to practise as a GP in Pakistan. Make sure you know local priorities well:
- Infections: tuberculosis (including DOTS and drug-resistant TB), typhoid (including XDR typhoid), dengue, malaria, hepatitis B and C, rabies, tetanus, diarrhoeal disease.
- Maternal and child health: antenatal care, anaemia in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, PPH, neonatal resuscitation, the Pakistan EPI schedule, malnutrition, IMCI.
- Emergencies: organophosphate poisoning, snake bite, heat stroke, road traffic trauma, burns.
- Chronic disease: diabetes, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, CKD, thalassaemia.
- Community Medicine: screening, outbreak investigation, immunisation, biostatistics calculations.
- Forensic Medicine: injuries, post-mortem changes, poisoning and medicolegal duties.

articles.title: How to use this app
lines: - Practice: work through each subject in short sets. Answers and explanations show straight away. Practice questions never appear in the mocks.
- Mocks: 10 papers of 200 questions, weighted like the real theory paper. The timer pauses if you leave, and your answers are saved.
- Results: your overall score against the 60% pass line, clinical and basic sciences totals, every subject, and the topics to work on.
- Review: read every explanation after a mock, especially the questions you got wrong or skipped.
- Progress: track your mock scores and your weakest topics over time.
All questions are original practice material written for this app. They are not real or recalled NRE questions.

articles.title: Preparing for the CSE
lines: Once you pass theory, start CSE preparation early. It needs practice, not just reading.
- Practise history taking and explaining things to patients in plain language, in Urdu and English.
- Rehearse systematic examinations: cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, neurological, and obstetric and gynaecological.
- Practise interpreting ECGs, X-rays, ABGs and blood results quickly.
- Learn the steps of common procedures: cannulation, catheterisation, suturing, basic life support and neonatal resuscitation.
- Practise against an 8-minute timer with a colleague acting as patient and examiner.
- Find out from PM&DC notices which stations are mandatory for your session, and make sure you are safe in all of them.
